books.section: America Transformed into the Industrial Giant of the World (1870–1910)
Industrialization, Corporate Consolidation, and the Gospel of Wealth

primary_sources: Booker T. Washington, Atlanta Exposition address, September 18, 1895

stimulus.text: One-third of the population of the South is of the Negro race. … As we have proved our loyalty to you in the past, in nursing your children, watching by the sick-bed of your mothers and fathers, and often following them with tear-dimmed eyes to their graves, so in the future, in our humble way, we shall stand by you with a devotion that no foreigner can approach, ready to lay down our lives, if need be, in defense of yours, interlacing our industrial, commercial, civil, and religious life with yours in a way that shall make the interests of both races one. In all things that are purely social we can be as separate as the fingers, yet one as the hand in all things essential to mutual progress.
stimulus.source_note: Booker T. Washington, Atlanta Exposition address, September 18, 1895. Public domain; wording and punctuation follow The Booker T. Washington Papers, vol. 3. Ellipsis marks an omission between complete sentences.

stem: Washington accepts being “as separate as the fingers” in “all things that are purely social.” What does this show about his strategy?

options.text: He believed social equality had already been won
options.misconception: Washington accepts separation, which means social equality had not been won.

options.text: He wanted the federal government to end segregation at once
options.misconception: Washington asks for no federal action here; he accepts social separation.

options.text: He accepted social separation while seeking progress through economic cooperation
He believed Black Southerners should leave the United States
options.misconception: Washington urges Black Southerners to stay and build in the South.

rationales.A: Accepting separation shows social equality had not been won.
rationales.B: Washington seeks progress through work together, not through federal action now.
rationales.C: Washington accepts the fingers apart and the hand together: separate socially, one in work.
rationales.D: Washington’s speech is about building a life in the South, not leaving.
rationales.general:
Hold the two halves of the image together.
1. The fingers are separate: in purely social things, the races stay apart.
2. The hand is one: in work and progress, the races act together.
3. Washington trades immediate social equality for economic cooperation.
4. Background from the books: critics called this the Atlanta Compromise, and Du Bois later challenged it.
Remember: a strategy can accept one thing to win another.
